## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāsārajātaka* (Ja 92) is a birth story belonging to the Ekanipāta of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1877]. The narrative was delivered by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana with reference to the Venerable Ānanda [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta acts as a wise minister (*paṇḍita-amacca*) who solves the mysterious theft of royal jewels by identifying a female monkey as the real culprit [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877]. Impressed by this clever discernment, the king honors the Bodhisatta and utters the canonical verse (*gāthā*) beginning *Ukkaṭṭhe sūram icchanti* (“For war men crave...”; “They desire a hero in battle; in counselors, freedom from panic”) [SuttaCentral; Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the king of that lifetime is identified as Ānanda and the wise minister as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1877].

An abridged version of the prologue to this Jātaka is preserved in the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary to the *Saṁyutta Nikāya*, where it provides the background narrative concerning the loss of royal ornaments [Rhys Davids 1917; Bhikkhu Bodhi 2003].

Neither SuttaCentral nor the computational analysis of DharmaNexus records any internal Pali text-reuse or cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Tibetan, or Chinese Āgamas for this Jātaka [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
